name: Zynum
workload: GEMM GFLOP/s over 42 NN column-major shapes for each of sgemm/dgemm/cgemm/zgemm (168 cases), six interleaved fresh-process runs per library, on an Apple M5 with 10 threads.
claimed_speedup: sgemm 1024x1024x1024: 1998.7 GFLOP/s vs OpenBLAS 472.6 and Accelerate 1924.8; dgemm sq1024: 556.5 vs OpenBLAS 252.4 and Accelerate 505.8 (gemm.csv). Median Zynum/OpenBLAS GFLOP/s ratio over all 168 cases is 2.15x (derived from page data), Zynum faster in 146 of 168 cases. Versus Accelerate the median ratio is 1.11x, with Zynum ahead in 100 of 168 cases (derived from page data) and behind on sgemm medians (0.93x).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0, zig build -Dcpu=baseline -Ddispatch=dynamic -Doptimize=ReleaseFast; OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=10 OPENBLAS_DYNAMIC=0; OpenBLAS 0.3.34
hardware: Apple M5, 10 logical CPUs, macOS 27.0 (feat_sme/sme2 detected)
tradeoffs: Zig-native BLAS exposing CBLAS and Fortran-ABI entry points plus C headers (include <zynum/blas/cblas.h>, link zynum_blas), so it is callable from C++. Needs Zig 0.16 to build. LGPL-3.0-or-later (GPL-3.0 text also shipped). Level 1-3 BLAS only; no LAPACK. Beta, API and dispatch policy may change.
caveats: Single host (Apple M5), measurements by the author. Zynum appears to dispatch SME/AArch64 kernels while OpenBLAS 0.3.34 on M5 likely runs NEON kernels, which probably explains the 3.9x median sgemm gap; Accelerate (Apple's vendor BLAS) is the fairer comparator and Zynum is roughly even to slightly slower on sgemm/dgemm medians (0.93x and 0.99x of Accelerate's GFLOP/s). Some shapes (e.g. m17_n2048_k257) are slower than both rivals (sgemm 107.2 vs Accelerate 429.1, OpenBLAS 203.5 GFLOP/s). The dataset is marked dirty (uncommitted working-tree sources hashed in source.json), correctness is sampled-checked only, and the metadata reader reports a kernel_coverage_invalid_document diagnostic. Repo is days-to-weeks old with no external users. Level 2 timings include Python/ctypes overhead.

name: Octavian.jl
workload: Dense matrix multiplication GFLOPS across sizes 10 to 1000 (square), run with BLASBenchmarksCPU.jl; headline row is 1000x1000x1000 with 36 threads.
claimed_speedup: 1000x1000x1000: Octavian median 1816 GFLOPS (max 1895) vs OpenBLAS median 1254 (max 1385), MKL median 1348 (max 1589), BLIS median 1051 (max 1476). README states 'Octavian has the fastest CPU performance' among the listed Julia packages.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.7.0-DEV.1124 (2021-05-19), LLVM 11.0.1 ORCJIT cascadelake, JULIA_NUM_THREADS=36; benchmark via BLASBenchmarksCPU.jl (public)
tradeoffs: Pure Julia, built on LoopVectorization.jl; BLAS-like gemm-style API (matmul) rather than a full BLAS/LAPACK ABI, so it is not directly callable from C++. Task scheduling can interfere with Base.Threads tasks (README docs note).
caveats: The headline figure is from one 2021 run on a 36-thread Skylake-X/Cascade Lake part with a Julia dev build; MKL and OpenBLAS may be better tuned for other sizes or newer versions. The README says the full size sweep took 2h25m. Newer LoopVectorization/Julia versions may change results. Not a C++-callable library.

name: PureBLAS.jl
baseline: OpenBLAS (Julia's bundled build) and AOCL-BLIS (AMD's BLIS fork); the repo's gate is max(OpenBLAS, AOCL)
workload: Single-threaded Float64 and ComplexF64 BLAS 1-3 and LAPACK routines across sizes on three AMD microarchitectures (2619 op/size/machine cells), measured with ABBA-interleaved rounds at locked clock frequency and the median ratio reported.
claimed_speedup: README: about 87% of benchmarked cells are at or above max(OpenBLAS, AOCL), single-threaded. Median PureBLAS/OpenBLAS ratios (Zen3/Zen4/Zen5) from bench/gen_table.md: gemm 1.17/1.08/1.23, potrf 1.11/1.46/1.49, geqrf 1.55/1.79/1.66, getrf 1.17/1.20/1.31, gesvd 1.30/1.27/1.30, syev 1.40/1.44/1.34. Versus AOCL (gen_table_aocl.md): gemm 1.06/1.08/1.07, potrf 1.72/1.37/1.20, geqrf 1.64/1.30/1.24. notes.md: gemm at n=4096 is 1.252/1.280/1.308 (Zen4/Zen3/Zen5) against the faster of OpenBLAS and AOCL.
compiler_and_flags: Julia (README requires Julia 1.13) with LLVM; benchmark is `taskset -c N julia --project=bench bench/plots.jl bench` with BLAS.set_num_threads(1) and frequency locking via bench/fleet_freqlock.sh (methodology.md); no extra compiler flags stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X (Zen3), Ryzen 5 7640U (Zen4), Ryzen AI 5 340 (Zen5); measured 2026-09-23 (bench/provenance.md)
tradeoffs: Pure Julia BLAS and LAPACK (about 36k lines) that derives block sizes from detected cache and vector sizes. Inside Julia it reroutes LinearAlgebra through libblastrampoline with PureBLAS.activate(). It can also build libpureblas.so (ILP64 BLAS symbols, embedded Julia runtime) via juliac --trim, which the README calls experimental; that route makes it linkable from C/C++/Rust. Single-threaded only (multithreading deliberately on hold). Singular vectors only for Float64 and complex.
caveats: All measurements are the author's, on AMD hardware only (no Intel), single-threaded, Float64/ComplexF64 only. The win over OpenBLAS is larger than over AOCL, and roughly 13% of cells are below the gate (listed in docs/src/notes.md; some trmm/trsm/solve cells are 0.78-0.94 of AOCL). About 30% of cells sit within +-5% of parity and the methodology page says run-to-run noise moves the below-gate count by 10-15 cells per sweep. notes.md says large-n gemm uses Strassen-Winograd (1.2-1.4x at large n), which has weaker numerical error bounds than classical gemm. The OpenBLAS version and AOCL version are not stated in the pages read. Repository is days old (first visible commits 2026-09-26) with 0 forks and no external users.

name: MaxMulSK
baseline: OpenBLAS (tuned build reaching its own SME kernels, one thread) and Apple Accelerate
workload: Single-thread FP32 GEMM over 35 shapes (squares, LLM-shaped, DeepSeek-V3 and LLaMA shapes) with allocation, packing and writeback inside every timed call, on an Apple M4 using Arm SME2.
claimed_speedup: README: v5.1 (development kernel, code not yet published) is 1.86x tuned OpenBLAS (geometric mean of paired ratios, ahead on 33 of 35 shapes, tied on 2) and 1.16x Apple Accelerate (behind at 256^3: 0.74x). For the published v3 kernel (2026-09-09 session): 1.40 to 1.77 TFLOP/s end to end on squares 256^3 to 4096^3, 1.01x to 1.31x OpenBLAS on squares and 1.36x to 2.23x on LLM shapes, but 5 to 17% behind Accelerate at most sizes.
compiler_and_flags: LLVM/Clang from Homebrew, CMake with -O3 -mcpu=apple-m4 -march=armv8.7-a+sme+sme2 (CMakeLists.txt); OpenBLAS thread count 1 (OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1, OPENBLAS_DIRECT_LIMIT=1792), Accelerate pinned to one thread via BLASSetThreading
tradeoffs: C++20 library for Apple M4 only (needs SME/SME2); single-threaded FP32 row-major C = A*B with packing and blocking done internally; Homebrew clang and libomp required. Not a BLAS ABI drop-in.
caveats: The headline v5.1 numbers are from kernel code that is not yet in the repository (published code is v3 and v4c), so only the v3/v4c claims are reproducible from the repo. Versus Accelerate (Apple's own SME-aware BLAS) the margin is 1.16x geomean and it loses at small sizes; the 1.86x figure is against an OpenBLAS build the README says reaches its SME kernels only when built from develop with DYNAMIC_ARCH (the stock Homebrew build cannot). Small-size results depend on call order (matrix-unit frequency effects), acknowledged in the README. Single M4 machine, author's measurements, zero stars.

name: apple-bottom
baseline: Apple Accelerate DGEMM on AMX (and OpenBLAS 6-thread in a Quantum ESPRESSO run)
workload: DGEMM GFLOP/s using double-float (FP32 pair) arithmetic on Metal GPU kernels versus the CPU Accelerate AMX path, plus end-to-end Quantum ESPRESSO Si64 wall time.
claimed_speedup: M2 Max: DGEMM 2048^2 552 GFLOP/s vs Accelerate 468 (+18%), 4096^2 643 vs 566 (+14%). Quantum ESPRESSO Si64: 2:01 with apple-bottom vs 2:28 with OpenBLAS 6-thread (22% faster wall time, 47% less CPU usage); Si128 +12% wall.
hardware: Apple M2 Max (38-core GPU, 64 GB unified memory)
tradeoffs: Metal compute shaders with a C API (apple_bottom.h) and a Fortran bridge that routes calls under 100M FLOPs to OpenBLAS/Accelerate and large calls to the GPU; callable from C++. Not IEEE FP64: precision is about 1e-15 (double-float), so results are not bit-exact; ZHERK is slower than the CPU path; single calls under N=1024 are dominated by about 100 us GPU overhead; max dimension 46,340.
caveats: First-party numbers on one machine with no compiler flags or methodology details; margins are modest (+14-18%) against Accelerate, which is not in the category baseline list; the OpenBLAS comparison is an application-level run on 6 threads rather than a GEMM microbenchmark. Double-float arithmetic is not equivalent to native FP64, and the README warns against it for pivoted LU and eigensolvers. Last commit is about five months old.

name: fast-matmul (Benson and Ballard)
workload: Sequential square dgemm (N = 1000 to 7500) comparing MKL against Strassen and other fast matrix multiplication algorithms with 1 to 3 recursion levels; run times in ms, median of five trials, data checked into data/all_sequential_algs/square.all.big.
claimed_speedup: Derived from page data: Strassen with 2 recursion levels takes 4836 ms vs MKL 5361 ms at N=4000 (1.11x) and 15790 ms vs 18075 ms at N=6000 (1.14x); 3 levels 15561 ms at N=6000 (1.16x); 1.04x at N=2000. The PPoPP 2015 paper (cited in README) reports better performance than MKL dgemm on a shared-memory machine.
compiler_and_flags: C++11 with OpenMP and Intel MKL; flags set in make.incs/make.inc.linux (not read)
hardware: NERSC Edison (data/README.md says all data was collected on Edison; sequential results should be scaled to 3.2 GHz because of Turbo Boost); CPU model not stated in the files read
tradeoffs: Code-generated implementations of Strassen, Bini (approximate) and many other fast algorithms for sequential and shared-memory parallel use, calling MKL for base cases; requires MKL. Fast algorithms have weaker numerical stability (README reports errors about 1e-14 to 1e-15 for exact algorithms and larger for approximate ones) and only win for large matrices.
caveats: The 1.11-1.16x figures are derived from raw timing files and exclude the approximate (Bini) algorithm, which is faster still but numerically lossy; some rows in the data are noisy (for example one-level Strassen at N=1000 takes 405.8 ms vs 108.2 ms for MKL). The speedup applies only to N of about 2000 and above, and the machine is a 2014-era supercomputer node, so the ratio against current MKL on modern CPUs is unknown. The paper itself (arXiv 1409.2908) could not be opened here (arxiv.org blocked); the paper claim is from the README citation and a search snippet.
